notes.front: What is denial of service (DoS)?
notes.back: The prevention of authorised access to resources, or the delaying of time-critical operations.
notes.explanation: What counts as time-critical depends on the service: it may be milliseconds or it may be hours.
notes.example: Like jamming a shop’s door so customers cannot get in, but done to a network service.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1, An Introduction to Information Security, Appendix B Glossary, “Denial of Service”, PDF p. 88
notes.evidence: Denial of Service The prevention of authorized access to resources or the delaying of time-critical operations. (Time-critical may be milliseconds or it may be hours, depending upon the service provided).

notes.front: What is a distributed denial of service (DDoS) attack?
notes.back: A denial-of-service attack whose traffic is generated from many distributed sources and directed at one intended victim.
notes.explanation: Using many sources lets the attacker achieve a high-volume attack against the victim system or server.
notes.example: Like thousands of people ringing one shop’s phone at once so real customers cannot get through.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-189, Resilient Interdomain Traffic Exchange: BGP Security and DDoS Mitigation, §3.1 Spoofed Source Addresses, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: Distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) is a form attack where the attack traffic is generated from many distributed sources to achieve a high-volume attack and directed towards an intended victim (i.e., system or server)

notes.front: What is an amplification attack?
notes.back: An attack that reflects traffic off poorly administered open internet servers, multiplying the volume reaching the victim by 50 times or more.
notes.explanation: NIST says it is often combined with source address spoofing, with open time and name-lookup servers as examples.
notes.example: Like sending hundreds of catalogue requests in a neighbour’s name, so heavy parcels pile up on their doorstep.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-189, Resilient Interdomain Traffic Exchange: BGP Security and DDoS Mitigation, §3.2 Reflection Amplification Attacks, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: Source address spoofing is often combined with reflection and amplification from poorly administered open internet servers (e.g., DNS, NTP) to multiply the attack traffic volume by a factor of 50 or more

notes.front: What is source address validation (SAV)?
notes.back: An anti-spoofing technique that checks the source addresses of IP packets.
notes.explanation: NIST presents it among the techniques for deterring DDoS attacks that use spoofed addresses, and calls it effective.
notes.example: Like a post room refusing to send any letter whose return address is not the company’s own.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-189, Resilient Interdomain Traffic Exchange: BGP Security and DDoS Mitigation, §5 Securing Against DDoS & Reflection Amplification, PDF p. 38
notes.evidence: There are various existing techniques and recommendations for deterrence against DDoS attacks with spoofed addresses [BCP38] [BCP84] [NABCOP] [CSRIC4-WG5]. Source address validation (SAV) of internet protocol (IP) packets is an effective anti-spoofing technique

notes.front: What is a man-in-the-middle attack (MITM)?
notes.back: An attack performed to intercept and modify communications between two parties.
notes.explanation: NIST advises planning on the assumption that the networks between a remote worker’s device and the organisation cannot be trusted.
notes.example: Like a postal worker who opens letters, rewrites them and reseals them before delivery.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-46 Rev. 2, Guide to Enterprise Telework, Remote Access, and BYOD Security, §2.1 Vulnerabilities, Threats, and Security Controls, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: Man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks may also be performed to intercept and modify communications. Organizations should plan their remote access security on the assumption that the networks between the telework client device and the organization cannot be trusted.

notes.front: What is DNS cache poisoning?
notes.back: Inserting a malicious answer into the cache of a recursive (caching) name server, for example with forged responses.
notes.explanation: A poisoned cache threatens the queries that stub resolvers and forwarding servers send to that server.
notes.example: Like slipping a false number into a receptionist’s phone list, so every caller who asks is given the wrong line.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-81r3, Secure Domain Name System (DNS) Deployment Guide, §4.1 Threats to Recursive/Forwarding Services, PDF p. 36
notes.evidence: A poisoned cache of a recursive name server (for queries that originate from a stub resolver or a forwarding recursive name server) • A recursive name server that is induced to query for a specific name, and forged responses are immediately sent to the server attempting to insert a malicious answer into the cache

notes.front: What are the Domain Name System Security Extensions (DNSSEC)?
notes.back: A standardised set of extensions to DNS for securing DNS protocol communications against compromise.
notes.explanation: NIST calls it one part of the wider field of DNS security, to be implemented alongside other best practices.
notes.example: Like a tamper-evident seal on a directory listing: you can tell it has not been altered, but anyone can still read it.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-81r3, Secure Domain Name System (DNS) Deployment Guide, §2.2.2 Using Encrypted DNS and Authentication to Protect the Protocol, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: The DNSSEC is a standardized set of extensions to DNS for securing DNS protocol communications against compromise. It is one part of the wider field of DNS security and should be implemented alongside other best practices and protocol features.

notes.front: What is a content distribution network (CDN)?
notes.back: A network that serves cached copies of content away from its source; NIST also calls it a content delivery network.
notes.explanation: NIST’s storage guide says such cached copies should keep at least the same security characteristics as the source data.
notes.example: Like a publisher keeping stock in shops across the country instead of posting every book from one warehouse.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-209, Security Guidelines for Storage Infrastructure, §4.4 Network Configuration (NC-SS-R16), PDF p. 55
notes.evidence: Cached copies (e.g., using content delivery network (CDN), replicas, and proxies) retaining at least the same security characteristics as the source data.

notes.front: What is an intrusion detection and prevention system (IDPS)?
notes.back: A system that identifies possible incidents, logs information about them, attempts to stop them and reports them to security administrators.
notes.explanation: It joins the two processes: intrusion prevention is intrusion detection plus attempting to stop the possible incidents detected.
notes.example: Like a security guard who not only watches the cameras and writes up what happens, but also locks the door on an intruder.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), §2.5 Summary, PDF p. 21
notes.evidence: Intrusion prevention is the process of performing intrusion detection and attempting to stop detected possible incidents. Intrusion detection and prevention systems (IDPS) are primarily focused on identifying possible incidents, logging information about them, attempting to stop them, and reporting them to security administrators.

notes.front: In many DDoS attacks the source addresses in the attack messages are spoofed. What for?
notes.back: To avoid traceability.
notes.explanation: Forged source addresses hide which machines really sent the attack traffic.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-189, Resilient Interdomain Traffic Exchange: BGP Security and DDoS Mitigation, §3.1 Spoofed Source Addresses, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: In many DDoS attacks, the IP source addresses in the attack messages are “spoofed” to avoid traceability

notes.front: Must a DDoS attack spoof its source addresses?
notes.back: No: in the Mirai attacks, a very large number of compromised Internet of Things devices used their normal source addresses.
notes.explanation: NIST notes that some DDoS attacks are launched without spoofed addresses at all.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-189, Resilient Interdomain Traffic Exchange: BGP Security and DDoS Mitigation, §3.1 Spoofed Source Addresses, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: Some DDoS attacks are launched without using spoofed source addresses. For example, in the Mirai attacks [Mirai1] [Mirai2] This publication is available free of charge from: https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-189 [Winward] [TA16-288A], a very large number of compromised bots (IoT devices) sending the attack traffic used the normal source IP addresses of the IoT devices.

notes.front: In NIST’s table of UDP protocols abused for amplification, what factor does the Network Time Protocol reach, compared with name lookup?
notes.back: About 557 for the Network Time Protocol, against 28 to 54 for the Domain Name System.
notes.explanation: The factor is the traffic multiplier an attacker can achieve by exploiting each protocol’s reflection and amplification effect over UDP.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-189, Resilient Interdomain Traffic Exchange: BGP Security and DDoS Mitigation, §5.4 Table 1: Common Applications and their TCP/UDP Port Numbers, PDF p. 47
notes.evidence: Domain Name System (DNS) 28 to 54 53, 853, 953 Official Network Time Protocol (NTP) 557 123 Official

notes.front: A company’s internet link is swamped by large name-lookup responses from thousands of open resolvers, answering queries the company never sent. What is happening?
notes.back: A: A reflection and amplification DDoS, using queries that carry the company’s address as a forged source.
notes.choices:
A) A reflection and amplification DDoS, using queries that carry the company’s address as a forged source
B) A man-in-the-middle attack on the company’s link
C) DNS cache poisoning of the company’s own resolver
D) A misconfigured firewall on the company’s side
notes.choicesExplained: C: cache poisoning inserts false answers into a resolver’s cache; it does not flood a link. B: a MITM intercepts and modifies communications rather than flooding them. D: a firewall cannot cause strangers’ servers to send the company responses.
notes.explanation: Open servers direct their responses to the target because the target’s address was forged as the source of the requests.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-189, Resilient Interdomain Traffic Exchange: BGP Security and DDoS Mitigation, §3.2 Reflection Amplification Attacks, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: The responses from such open internet servers are directed to the attack target since the target’s IP address was forged as the source address field of the request messages.

notes.front: What are two techniques used to implement source address validation?
notes.back: Ingress and egress access control lists, and unicast Reverse Path Forwarding.
notes.explanation: NIST says SAV is performed in network edge devices, such as border routers.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-189, Resilient Interdomain Traffic Exchange: BGP Security and DDoS Mitigation, §5.1 Source Address Validation Techniques, PDF p. 38
notes.evidence: Source address validation (SAV) is performed in network edge devices, such as border routers, cable modem termination systems (CMTS) [RFC4036], digital subscriber line access multiplexers (DSLAM), and packet data network gateways (PDN-GW) in mobile networks [Firmin]. Ingress/egress access control lists (ACLs) and unicast Reverse Path Forwarding (uRPF) are techniques employed for implementing SAV

notes.front: Ingress versus egress source address validation: which packets does each apply to?
notes.back: Ingress: incoming (received) packets. Egress: outgoing (transmitted) packets.
notes.explanation: The same validation can be applied to traffic in either direction.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-189, Resilient Interdomain Traffic Exchange: BGP Security and DDoS Mitigation, §5.1 Source Address Validation Techniques, PDF p. 38
notes.evidence: Ingress SAV applies to incoming (received) packets, and egress SAV applies to outgoing (transmitted) packets.

notes.front: Which outbound traffic does NIST’s firewall guide say an organisation should permit, to stop spoofed traffic leaking out?
notes.back: Only outbound traffic that uses the source IP addresses in use by the organisation.
notes.explanation: This egress filtering helps block traffic with spoofed addresses from leaking onto other networks.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, §2.1.1 Packet Filtering, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: Organizations should only permit outbound traffic that uses the source IP addresses in use by the organization—a process that helps block traffic with spoofed addresses from leaking onto other networks.

notes.front: An internet provider notices packets leaving one customer’s connection with source addresses that belong to other networks. What should its egress filter on that customer interface do?
notes.back: A: Permit only source addresses from the address space associated with that customer’s interface, and drop the rest.
notes.choices:
A) Permit only source addresses from the address space associated with that customer’s interface, and drop the rest
B) Permit all packets, since filtering is the customer’s job
C) Rewrite the source addresses to the provider’s own
D) Rate-limit the packets but still forward them
notes.choicesExplained: B: NIST places egress filtering on the provider’s access devices. C: rewriting addresses hides the problem and still forwards the traffic. D: rate-limiting still lets spoofed packets through.
notes.explanation: Egress access control lists typically permit only the prefixes associated with the interface where the customer network connects.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-189, Resilient Interdomain Traffic Exchange: BGP Security and DDoS Mitigation, §5.1.1 SAV Using Access Control Lists, PDF p. 38
notes.evidence: Typically, the egress ACLs in access aggregation devices (e.g., CMTS, DSLAM, PDN-GW) permit source addresses only from the address spaces (prefixes) that are associated with the interface on which the customer network is connected.

notes.front: An enterprise finds its internal DNS resolver answering queries from anyone on the internet, and it has been used in amplification attacks. Its real clients are all on the enterprise network. What should it do?
notes.back: A: Keep access lists on the resolver so it accepts requests only from its own clients, making it effectively closed.
notes.choices:
A) Keep access lists on the resolver so it accepts requests only from its own clients, making it effectively closed
B) Move the resolver to a different port
C) Add more bandwidth so the attacks do less harm
D) Enable DNSSEC signing of its zones
notes.choicesExplained: D: DNSSEC protects the integrity of DNS data; it does not stop strangers using the resolver. B: a new port does not limit who can send requests. C: more bandwidth does not stop the resolver amplifying attacks on others.
notes.explanation: NIST says an internal resolver can limit the clients it accepts requests from, usually those inside the same network, so an open resolver becomes closed.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-189, Resilient Interdomain Traffic Exchange: BGP Security and DDoS Mitigation, §5.4 Monitoring UDP/TCP Ports… and Employing Traffic Filtering, PDF p. 46
notes.evidence: the enterprise internal DNS resolver can limit the scope of clients from which it will accept requests. The clients normally come from within the same enterprise network where the DNS resolver resides. Hence, the DNS recursive resolver can maintain access lists in the configuration so that an otherwise open DNS resolver can be effectively “closed”

notes.front: How can a MITM downgrade a mail connection that uses STARTTLS?
notes.back: It intercepts the server’s reply to a connection request and scrubs out the STARTTLS request.
notes.explanation: This downgrade attack works when STARTTLS is initiated as a request by the server side.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-177 Rev. 1, Trustworthy Email, §5.2.4 STARTTLS, PDF p. 76
notes.evidence: it may be susceptible to a downgrade attack, where a man-in-the-middle (MITM) is in place. In this case the MITM receives the STARTTLS request from the server reply to a connection request and scrubs it out.

notes.front: A consultant works from café Wi-Fi. Someone on the same network could intercept and alter her traffic to the office. What assumption does NIST say the organisation should plan on?
notes.back: D: That the networks between her device and the organisation cannot be trusted.
notes.choices:
A) That the café’s Wi-Fi password keeps the traffic private
B) That interception is possible only on wired networks
C) That attacks are only likely on the office network
D) That the networks between her device and the organisation cannot be trusted
notes.choicesExplained: A: a shared password does not protect her from others on the same network. C: NIST points to the networks in between, not the office network. B: NIST lists wireless networks among those susceptible to eavesdropping.
notes.explanation: MITM attacks may be performed to intercept and modify communications, so NIST plans remote security on the networks in between being untrusted.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-46 Rev. 2, Guide to Enterprise Telework, Remote Access, and BYOD Security, §2.1 Vulnerabilities, Threats, and Security Controls, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: Man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks may also be performed to intercept and modify communications. Organizations should plan their remote access security on the assumption that the networks between the telework client device and the organization cannot be trusted.

notes.front: What are two attacks that NIST says can poison the cache of a recursive name server?
notes.back: Any two of: packet interception; guessing the request’s identifier field and query; responses from a compromised authoritative name server.
notes.explanation: In packet interception, the attacker spoofs a name server and answers before the real response arrives.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-81r3, Secure Domain Name System (DNS) Deployment Guide, §4.1 Threats to Recursive/Forwarding Services, PDF p. 37
notes.evidence: Packet interception. The attacker eavesdrops on a request and sends a response by spoofing a name server before the real response from the legitimate name server reaches the recursive name server.

notes.front: To mitigate attacks such as cache poisoning, how should a recursive name server be run relative to an authoritative one?
notes.back: Under a different security policy from the authoritative name server.
notes.explanation: NIST gives cache poisoning as the example attack this separation mitigates.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-81r3, Secure Domain Name System (DNS) Deployment Guide, §2.3 Name Server Roles, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: A recursive name server should be run under a different security policy than that of an authoritative name server to mitigate attacks (e.g., cache poisoning).

notes.front: What cryptography does DNSSEC use, and to produce what?
notes.back: Public-key cryptography, to generate digital signatures over DNS data.
notes.explanation: The current set of signing algorithms is defined in a separate standard that lists the mandatory and optional ones.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-81r3, Secure Domain Name System (DNS) Deployment Guide, §3.8.1 DNSSEC Key Considerations, PDF p. 31
notes.evidence: DNSSEC is based on public-key cryptography to generate digital signatures over DNS data. The current set of cryptographic algorithms is defined in RFC 8624 [21], which lists the mandatory and optional algorithms supported by DNSSEC tools.

notes.front: What two tasks does configuring DNSSEC validation on a resolver require?
notes.back: Configuring the server to perform validation, and configuring one or more trusted public keys as trust anchors.
notes.explanation: The method for both depends on the DNS implementation used.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-81r3, Secure Domain Name System (DNS) Deployment Guide, §4.2.5 Enabling DNSSEC Validation, PDF p. 41
notes.evidence: Configuring DNSSEC validation requires two tasks: configuring the server to perform validation and configuring one or more trusted public keys to act as trust anchors. The method for achieving this depends on the DNS implementation used.

notes.front: DNSSEC versus DNS over TLS: what does each protect?
notes.back: DNSSEC protects the integrity of DNS communications; DNS over TLS, like other encrypted DNS, provides confidentiality and privacy.
notes.explanation: NIST says DNSSEC gives no confidentiality or privacy protection, and names encrypted DNS as the technologies that do.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-81r3, Secure Domain Name System (DNS) Deployment Guide, §2.2.2 Using Encrypted DNS and Authentication to Protect the Protocol, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: While DNSSEC can help protect against the compromise of DNS communications (i.e., integrity protection), it does not provide any confidentiality or privacy protection. Those capabilities are provided by other technologies, such as DNS over Transport Layer Security (TLS) (DoT), DNS over Secure Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTPS) (DoH), and DNS over Quick UDP Internet Connections (QUIC) (DoQ)

notes.front: Staff are being sent to a fake payroll site because their company’s caching resolver holds forged answers for the payroll domain. Which countermeasure lets the resolver detect forged DNS data?
notes.back: C: Enable DNSSEC validation on the resolver.
notes.choices:
A) Switch staff to DNS over TLS only
B) Block UDP port 53 at the firewall
C) Enable DNSSEC validation on the resolver
D) Add a content distribution network in front of the payroll site
notes.choicesExplained: A: encrypted DNS protects confidentiality on the path to the resolver; it does not authenticate the data the resolver has cached. B: blocking name lookup breaks it rather than checking it. D: a CDN serves cached copies of the site but cannot stop the resolver handing out a false address.
notes.explanation: DNSSEC was designed to provide authentication for DNS data, which is what a validating resolver checks.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-81r3, Secure Domain Name System (DNS) Deployment Guide, §4.2 Recommendations for Protection, PDF p. 37
notes.evidence: DNSSEC was designed to provide authentication for DNS data but does not protect the confidentiality of DNS query/response transactions.

notes.front: In NIST’s threat-sharing guide, what do companies facing a DDoS campaign enlist content distribution providers to do?
notes.back: Deploy DDoS-resistant web architectures.
notes.explanation: They decide this after a technical exchange meeting among the targeted companies.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-150, Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing, Scenario 3: Distributed Denial of Service Attack, PDF p. 36
notes.evidence: After a technical exchange meeting among the targeted companies, several companies decide to enlist the services of content distribution providers to deploy DDoS-resistant web architectures.

notes.front: A charity expects a hacktivist group to flood its donation website with traffic during a televised appeal. Which countermeasure matches this threat?
notes.back: C: Use a content distribution provider to deploy a DDoS-resistant web architecture.
notes.choices:
A) Require multi-factor authentication for staff sign-ins
B) Enable DNSSEC on the charity’s domain
C) Use a content distribution provider to deploy a DDoS-resistant web architecture
D) Change the website to a non-standard port
notes.choicesExplained: B: DNSSEC protects the integrity of DNS data, not a site’s capacity. A: multi-factor authentication protects sign-ins; it adds no capacity against a flood aimed at the website. D: the flood would simply follow the site to its new port.
notes.explanation: NIST describes content distribution providers deploying DDoS-resistant web architectures for organisations targeted by DDoS.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-150, Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing, Scenario 3: Distributed Denial of Service Attack, PDF p. 36
notes.evidence: several companies decide to enlist the services of content distribution providers to deploy DDoS-resistant web architectures.

notes.front: When an IDPS responds to a detected threat, what are two response techniques it can use?
notes.back: Any two of: stopping the attack itself; changing the security environment, such as reconfiguring a firewall; changing the attack’s content.
notes.explanation: Many IDPSs can respond this way, attempting to prevent a detected threat from succeeding.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), Executive Summary, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: Many IDPSs can also respond to a detected threat by attempting to prevent it from succeeding. They use several response techniques, which involve the IDPS stopping the attack itself, changing the security environment (e.g., reconfiguring a firewall), or changing the attack’s content.

notes.front: Which type of IDPS examines network traffic for threats that generate unusual traffic flows, such as DDoS attacks?
notes.back: Network behaviour analysis.
notes.explanation: NIST also lists certain forms of malicious code and policy violations among the unusual flows it looks for.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), Executive Summary, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: Network Behavior Analysis (NBA), which examines network traffic to identify threats that generate unusual traffic flows, such as distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks, certain forms of malware, and policy violations

notes.front: A university wants extra detection for floods of traffic that could signal a denial-of-service attack across its internal networks. Which IDPS technology does NIST say to add for this?
notes.back: B: Network behaviour analysis.
notes.choices:
A) Host-based
B) Network behaviour analysis
C) Wireless
D) None: an IDPS cannot detect denial of service
notes.choicesExplained: A: host-based IDPSs monitor a single host’s characteristics and events. C: wireless IDPSs watch wireless networking protocols. D: NIST names denial of service among the threats this type is particularly well suited to detect.
notes.explanation: NIST says these technologies can be deployed when an organisation wants additional detection for denial-of-service attacks.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), Executive Summary, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: NBA technologies can also be deployed if organizations desire additional detection capabilities for denial of service attacks, worms, and other threats that NBAs are particularly well-suited to detecting.
